bridges.mechanism: Sustained disruption of shipping (attacks, mines, seizures) provokes immediate naval escorts, interdiction operations, and counterstrikes by the US and partner navies as well as kinetic retaliation by Iran or proxies, raising the tempo and geographic spread of military engagements.

Repeated incidents affecting third‑party commercial vessels trigger formal protests, emergency consultations, sanctions threats, and coalition-building among affected states, increasing bilateral and multilateral diplomatic friction.

Acute shipping-route insecurity raises trade-finance and counterparty risk and forces dealers to hoard balance sheet and widen bid-ask spreads, directly reducing market depth and liquidity in fixed-income markets.

Worsening maritime disruption in the Persian Gulf/Red Sea raises freight rates, insurance premiums and forces rerouting and longer voyages that absorb global shipping capacity and cause delays and bottlenecks for sea‑borne deliveries (including weapons, spare parts and fuel) destined for Ukraine, increasing supply‑chain disruption supporting the war effort.

Repeated shipping disruptions tied to the Iran–US standoff raise perceived supply-chain and naval risk, prompting investors and defense buyers to channel additional capital into autonomous maritime systems, logistics AI and surveillance startups tied to US–China competition.

Heightened maritime insecurity drives rapid deployment of networked navigation, sensing and command AI for ships and coastal systems, creating high-value targets that elicit increased state and criminal cyber operations against AI assets in the US–China rivalry.

Sharp declines in crude transits through key chokepoints prompt affected producer and consumer states to use military means (escorts, interdictions, strikes) to reopen or secure routes, producing new or intensified kinetic operations in the maritime and littoral battlespace.
A drop in crude exports through key chokepoints cuts export receipts for producing countries and triggers sudden stops or reversals in capital flows as FX revenues and sovereign/NGP flows decline.

A fall in crude flow through key chokepoints reduces feedstock availability for refiners and cuts exportable refined products to Europe, directly tightening diesel and jet‑fuel availability for Ukrainian military and civilian needs and raising energy supply stress; conversely restoration of volumes eases that stress.

Acute declines in refined fuel availability (diesel, gasoline) disrupt transport, power and livelihoods in neighboring states and populated border areas, provoking protests, localized clashes over scarce supplies, and opportunistic militia violence that raises the rate of spillover incidents.

Higher commercial and strategic refined‑product inventories in Western suppliers enable continued bulk fuel deliveries, fuel-backed munitions and sustainment shipments for Ukrainian forces, whereas depletion forces allies to ration or postpone fuel‑dependent support, reducing effective military assistance.
A sustained rise in global oil prices lifts headline inflation and inflation expectations, prompting markets to price in earlier or higher central-bank policy tightening.
Oil-price spikes increase expected inflation and inflation risk premia independent of short-term policy moves, raising term premia and pushing up long-dated nominal government yields.

Intense policy responses (sanctions, emergency export controls, and redeployment orders) tied to an Iran–US standoff draw diplomatic focus and military assets to the Middle East and force allies to reallocate materiel, logistics and high-readiness assets away from programs and deliveries for Ukraine, reducing aggregate allied military assistance.

Aggressive energy-market interventions, sanctions or export curbs tied to the Iran–US standoff prompt reciprocal trade and security measures that broaden and intensify regulatory review and enforcement of cross-border AI investment and technology transfer.

A rapid increase in delivered weapons, ammunition, surveillance and targeting support enables recipient forces to conduct higher-tempo offensives and sustain engagements, directly raising the scale and frequency of kinetic operations.

Provision of offensive-capable systems (e.g., long‑range fires, air support) intensifies localized bombardment and territorial shifts that displace civilians and prompt cross-border flight independent of aggregate battle-space metrics.

Escalation signalled by greater allied military support intensifies sanctions risk and geopolitical uncertainty, triggering rapid reallocation of private and institutional capital into safe‑haven jurisdictions and sovereign assets, increasing measured cross‑border flows into those markets.

A surge in allied military support to Ukraine reallocates Western naval and air assets toward Europe (or increases forward operations that draw on the same assets), reducing deterrent presence in the Persian Gulf and enabling greater Iranian harassment/attacks on commercial shipping, raising maritime disruption.

Larger allied military assistance expands defense procurement and government R&D contracts for AI-enabled systems, which in turn channels increased public and private investment into AI firms and startups.

Acute energy shortages and price spikes prompt importing states to lodge formal protests, impose countermeasures or seek emergency supply deals, increasing bilateral and multilateral diplomatic frictions tied to the conflict.
War-related energy shortfalls and price spikes push up near-term CPI and headline inflation expectations, prompting markets to price in faster and larger central-bank tightening.
Sustained increases in energy prices raise inflation expectations and term premia on long-dated debt, directly lifting long‑term nominal government yields.
Disruptions to Russian hydrocarbon flows and related re-routing/risk premia from the Russia–Ukraine war tighten global supply and increase price risk, directly pushing up global crude prices.

Acute energy shortages and higher electricity prices raise datacenter and cloud costs, leading firms to delay or scale back rollouts of energy‑intensive autonomous agent services and thus reducing deployment rate.

Rising diplomatic friction (sanctions, expulsions, formal protests) prompts the US and partners to tighten export controls, screen foreign AI vendors, and open inquiries/enforcement actions, raising the intensity and scope of regulatory scrutiny in the US–China tech competition.

Interruptions to transport and spare‑parts flows reduce availability of munitions, fuel and maintenance, degrading operational sustainment and forcing reductions in sortie rates and tempo of ground operations.

Logistical and settlement frictions from disrupted shipping and trade increase trading volatility and operational risk, leading dealers to reduce inventories and widen bid‑ask spreads, tightening fixed‑income market liquidity.

Logistical disruptions from the Russia–Ukraine conflict (insurance shocks, port congestion and longer voyages) reduce available tanker capacity and cause rerouting or delays, lowering crude volumes actually transiting narrow chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz in the near term.

War-related interruptions to semiconductor and specialized hardware shipments reduce some developers' access to accelerators needed for large-scale training, slowing or downsizing model training and lowering average deployed model capability in affected actors.

A rapid rise in deployed model capability enables more autonomous ISR and precision strike systems and faster decision loops, lowering operational thresholds and increasing the tempo and scale of kinetic operations between rivals.

Rapid improvements in deployed AI model capabilities raise market forecasts for near-term productivity, growth and inflation, leading participants to price in higher expected future central bank policy rates.

Improvements in deployed AI model capability for maritime ISR, anomaly detection and autonomous reconnaissance raise effective monitoring and attribution of hostile acts, strengthening deterrence and reducing the incidence of small-boat harassment and other disruptions.

Rising average model capability—driven by rivalry-driven R&D—enables more effective planning, target recognition, and guidance tools that actors can use to select and strike energy infrastructure, increasing outages and stress on energy supplies supporting Ukraine and its neighbours as those tools are fielded.

Accelerated deployment of autonomous surveillance and enforcement agents along contested borders and in occupied areas increases rates of misidentification and accidental engagements, producing localized clashes and reprisals that spill into neighboring communities.

Faster deployment of agentic trading and risk-monitoring systems intensifies algorithmic responses to Iran–US incidents, causing larger, quicker repricing and upward spikes in oil markets when standoff signals appear.

Heightened AI-focused regulation, export controls and enforcement increase compliance costs and legal uncertainty for foreign investors, causing them to reduce or reroute cross-border capital into jurisdictions perceived as higher regulatory risk.

Tighter regulatory scrutiny and export-control rulemaking tied to US–China rivalry create licensing delays and legal barriers that directly slow or block transfers of AI-enabled systems (drones, targeting software, logistics AI) from allies to Ukraine, reducing effective military support in the near term.

A surge of capital into AI equities, private rounds and infrastructure diverts demand away from long-duration sovereign and high-grade fixed income (portfolio rebalancing) and increases term premia, putting upward pressure on long-term nominal yields.

Increased capital flows into AI firms accelerate production and scaling of ISR, autonomous effectors, and logistics optimization systems that allies can procure or donate, thereby raising the quantity and capability of military assistance available to Ukraine within a production and procurement cycle.

High-frequency, high-profile cyber intrusions against AI infrastructure and sensitive networks that are attributed (or publicly blamed) on the opposing side trigger formal protests, sanctions, and expulsions, directly elevating bilateral and multilateral diplomatic friction.

Targeted cyberattacks that disable power, water, logistics or humanitarian coordination systems in conflict zones precipitate acute civilian suffering and infrastructure collapse, driving rapid cross-border population movements.

Rising cyber exploits that hit trading platforms, market-making systems or critical data feeds cause trading outages and prompt liquidity providers to pull back or widen quotes, directly degrading fixed-income market liquidity.

A rise in cyber exploits against AI-enabled navigation, port-automation and logistics platforms increases the frequency of successful attacks that halt or degrade vessel traffic and port operations in the Persian Gulf and nearby chokepoints, producing measurable transit disruptions.

Increased successful cyber operations against oil terminal control systems, SCADA and tanker-management platforms directly degrade throughput and force temporary shutdowns, lowering crude export volumes transiting key chokepoints.

An uptick in malicious cyber activity aimed at AI components (optimization/automation systems for ports, freight management, and defense logistics) causes outages and data corruption that produce measurable delays and rerouting in weapons and humanitarian supply chains into the conflict zone.

A sustained rise in long-term yields raises sovereign borrowing costs and forces fiscally constrained governments to delay/curtail defense procurement and contractor payments, reducing operational tempo and lowering near-term kinetic intensity.

Higher long‑term yields increase the opportunity and financing costs of holding inventories for both commercial and strategic actors, prompting drawdowns or reduced purchases that lower refined fuel stock levels.

Rising long‑term sovereign yields increase governments' debt‑service and borrowing costs, constraining discretionary budgets and leading to slower, smaller or delayed external military assistance and procurement for partners supporting Ukraine.

A sustained rise in long-term nominal yields raises financing and pension costs for firms and public bodies, prompting near-term cuts to IT/security operating budgets and reducing patching and monitoring, which increases the frequency and success of cyber exploits against AI systems.

Rising market-implied future policy rates increase discount rates and borrowing costs, compress VC valuations and fundraising, and cause institutional investors to pull back from high-growth tech allocations, directly reducing new capital flowing into AI startups and infrastructure.

Acute illiquidity in global fixed-income markets precipitates disorderly sovereign bond moves and targeted losses for foreign investors, prompting formal protests, investigations or sanctions claims between affected states and raising bilateral diplomatic friction.

Tightening in fixed‑income market liquidity raises short‑term funding and trade‑finance costs (commercial paper, repos and market‑making) used by shippers, freight forwarders and suppliers, forcing inventory cuts and payment delays that produce immediate logistical and supply‑chain interruptions.

Severe tightening in fixed-income market liquidity disrupts corporate and cloud-provider treasury operations and credit-backed procurement, delaying purchases/rental of large-scale compute and data-center capacity needed for training cutting-edge models, thereby slowing near-term increases in model capability.

A sudden negative swing in cross-border capital flows (capital flight or remittance stoppage) sharply reduces household income and fiscal capacity in a fragile conflict zone, triggering rapid deterioration of services and livelihoods that drives people to cross borders seeking refuge.

Higher cross-border capital inflows improve availability of trade finance, letters of credit and marine insurance for exporters and traders, enabling more tanker loadings and increasing crude volumes transiting key chokepoints.

A sudden pullback in cross‑border capital flows reduces trade finance and working capital available to energy traders and operators, causing delayed cargoes, curtailed imports and increased short‑term stress in energy supply chains for importing countries.

A rise in investor risk appetite lowers insurer and carrier risk premia for transits through contested waters, reducing commercial rerouting and the frequency/intensity of operational disruptions reported at maritime chokepoints.

A decline in investor risk appetite raises the cost and reduces availability of corporate financing and export‑credit/insurance for defense manufacturers and exporters, slowing deliveries and reducing the pace or volume of allied materiel shipments to Ukraine.

A decline in investor and corporate risk appetite leads firms to postpone or scale back production rollouts of experimental agentic AI systems to avoid potential operational, reputational and liability risks, lowering deployment rates.

A rapid escalation of kinetic operations raises uncertainty and tail-risk perceptions, prompting institutional and retail investors to de-risk portfolios and increase allocations to safe assets, thereby lowering aggregate risk appetite.

Heightened conflict drives order imbalances and volatility in regionally exposed sovereign and corporate bonds while dealer balance-sheet constraints and repo funding stress reduce market depth and widen bid-ask spreads.

Intensified kinetic operations (naval strikes, air attacks, missile barrages) in or near the Gulf/Red Sea directly threaten commercial shipping and prompt route suspensions or convoying that immediately increases maritime transit disruptions.

A sharp rise in frontline fighting and materiel losses creates immediate operational needs and political pressure that prompt allies to accelerate and expand weapons, ammunition, and logistics deliveries to sustain the defending force.

Increased kinetic operations and strikes against export nodes (ports, pipelines, Black Sea shipping) physically reduce flows and force rerouting, producing near-term supply shortfalls and price spikes for regional energy markets.

A spike in kinetic conflict raises incentives and operational cover for state and proxy actors to launch cyber operations against adversary AI infrastructure (model endpoints, data pipelines, control systems) to degrade battlefield automation, increasing cyber exploit frequency and severity.

Substantial and sustained refugee inflows raise host-country near-term fiscal spending and expected future debt issuance, increasing sovereign risk premia and pushing up long-dated government yields in affected markets.

Large, fast refugee movements create urgent border-management and humanitarian processing needs that governments and NGOs meet by procuring and fielding agentic systems (surveillance drones, autonomous triage/translation agents), accelerating deployment rates.

Rising diplomatic friction (sanctions, trade restrictions, reputational risk) causes fast, anticipatory portfolio reallocation and withdrawal of cross-border funding from exposed jurisdictions into safe-haven markets, producing net outflows.

Escalating diplomatic friction among states involved in the standoff prompts governments to enact sanctions, export controls, or emergency energy measures (e.g., SPR releases), increasing the intensity and frequency of official energy-market interventions.

Escalating diplomatic confrontations and public condemnations raise domestic political incentives for allied governments to demonstrate resolve by increasing or fast-tracking military assistance packages.

Rising diplomatic friction between states triggers near-term government actions—export controls, entity listings, mandatory vendor reviews and expanded investigations—directly increasing the intensity and scope of regulatory scrutiny on rival-country AI firms and services.

Elevated diplomatic tensions drive investors and policymakers to favor domestic or allied AI companies (reshoring, sanctions avoidance, preferential procurement), diverting capital away from adversary-linked firms and increasing flows into national/regime-aligned AI projects.

Rising localized attacks and sabotage around ports, terminals, and pipelines adjacent to strategic chokepoints force temporary closures or reduced throughput, directly cutting crude export volumes through those chokepoints.

Localized violent incidents on border routes, rail lines, or at transshipment hubs interrupt freight movements and create chokepoints that degrade commercial and military logistics serving the conflict zone.

nodes.label: Sanctions enforcement tightness

nodes.label: Fuel‑economy regulation stringency

nodes.label: Export restriction likelihood

nodes.label: Corporate strategy reassessment rate
nodes.description: Speed and extent to which energy-sector firms adjust supply, investment and trading strategies in response to shocks.

nodes.label: Alternative fuel competitiveness

nodes.label: Consumer fuel cost burden
nodes.description: Share of household expenditure or income pressure attributable to prevailing fuel prices.

nodes.label: Strategic reserve liquidity
nodes.description: Available usable volume and legal/operational capacity of strategic petroleum reserves to be released or loaned.

nodes.label: Cyber attack frequency
nodes.description: The tempo of offensive cyberspace operations targeting networks, data centres and communications infrastructure.

nodes.label: Hybrid sabotage operation rate
nodes.description: The incidence of non‑kinetic sabotage and covert actions (forgery, arson, supply interdiction, covert strikes) intended to degrade opponents or third parties.

nodes.label: Critical communications disruption
nodes.description: The current level of functional impairment of critical communications and data infrastructure (connectivity, data centres, mobile networks).

nodes.label: Defense industry production capacity
nodes.description: The available industrial capacity to produce munitions, vehicles, airframes, electronic warfare systems and related defence materiel.

nodes.label: Allied military support level

nodes.label: Economic coercion pressure
nodes.description: The intensity of economic pressure measures (sanctions, asset freezes, banking restrictions, financial manipulation) deployed against actors connected to the conflict.

nodes.label: Energy supply stress
nodes.description: The degree of disruption and shortfall in energy supply chains, reflected in availability, price spikes and re-routing of deliveries.

nodes.label: Global market volatility
nodes.description: The level of financial and commodity market instability driven by conflict‑related shocks and uncertainty.

nodes.label: Defense force mobilization rate
nodes.description: The speed and scale at which armed forces expand personnel, activate reserves, and deploy units for operations.

nodes.label: Civilian displacement and casualty flow
nodes.description: The rate at which civilians are wounded, killed or displaced as a result of hostilities and related disruptions.

nodes.label: Public security perception
nodes.description: The population's perceived level of personal and societal security, including fear of attacks, sabotage or instability.

nodes.label: Diplomatic tension level
nodes.description: The intensity of diplomatic friction manifested through expulsions, formal protests, treaty suspensions and legal actions between states.

nodes.label: Legal and trade restrictions scope
nodes.description: The breadth and severity of formal trade, investment and legal restrictions applied to economic actors linked to the conflict.

nodes.label: Logistical and supply‑chain disruption
nodes.description: The current level of interruption to transport, shipping, and logistical networks that support commerce and military sustainment.

nodes.label: Agentic system deployment rate
nodes.description: The speed and volume at which agentic, autonomous AI systems are put into production or user-facing services.

nodes.label: Safety incident frequency
nodes.description: The rate at which safety failures, harmful outputs, or unintended behaviors from AI systems are observed or reported.

nodes.label: Regulatory scrutiny intensity
nodes.description: The intensity and breadth of regulatory attention, inquiries, rulemaking efforts and enforcement actions focused on AI.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite for AI
nodes.description: The willingness of investors and capital markets to accept risk and provide funding for AI ventures and projects.

nodes.label: Capital flow to AI projects
nodes.description: The volume and velocity of financial investment (VC, private equity, public markets) entering AI-related firms and infrastructure.

nodes.label: Market valuation pressure
nodes.description: Upward or downward pressure on valuations of AI companies and related assets driven by earnings expectations and risk repricing.

nodes.label: Public trust in AI
nodes.description: General public confidence and social license for AI technologies, including perceived safety, fairness and usefulness.

nodes.label: Openness of model ecosystem
nodes.description: The degree to which model weights, APIs, toolchains and implementation details are shared, permissive or closed.

nodes.label: Safety research activity
nodes.description: The rate and intensity of independent and internal research, audits, mitigations and tooling focused on AI safety and alignment.

nodes.label: Cyber exploit activity against AI
nodes.description: The frequency and severity of malicious cyber activity targeting AI models, accounts, data pipelines and deployed agents.

nodes.label: Legal liability risk expectation
nodes.description: Perceived likelihood and potential magnitude of legal claims, liability exposure and litigation stemming from AI harms.

nodes.label: Hardware supply capacity
nodes.description: Available compute, specialized chips and data‑center capacity that constrain AI training and deployment throughput.

nodes.label: AI talent supply level
nodes.description: The available pool of skilled engineers, researchers and operators capable of building and governing advanced AI systems.

nodes.label: Media attention intensity
nodes.description: The volume and prominence of media coverage, narrative salience and framing around AI topics and incidents.

nodes.label: Enterprise adoption rate
nodes.description: The pace at which businesses integrate AI capabilities into products, workflows and customer-facing services.

Long-term nominal yields
nodes.description: The prevailing market interest rates on long-dated government and similarly rated fixed-income instruments, measured as a continuous nominal yield level.

nodes.label: Headline inflation rate
nodes.description: The ongoing percentage change in a broad consumer price aggregate over a rolling period, capturing current inflationary pressure in the economy.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: The market and public anticipations of future inflation expressed as a continuous expectation level derived from surveys and market-implied metrics.

nodes.label: Policy rate expectations
nodes.description: The continuously varying market-implied expectation of future central policy interest rates over different horizons.

nodes.label: Oil price level
nodes.description: The spot or benchmark price level of crude oil, measured continuously as an index or currency-denominated price.

nodes.label: Term premium on long rates
nodes.description: The extra yield investors demand for holding long-dated bonds versus rolling short-term instruments, measured as a continuous premium component of yields.

nodes.label: Yield curve slope
nodes.description: The difference between longer- and shorter-maturity yields, measured continuously to capture curve steepness or inversion dynamics.

nodes.label: Fixed-income market liquidity
nodes.description: The prevailing ease and tightness of trading in fixed-income markets, measured by bid-ask spreads, market depth and transaction costs on a continuous scale.

nodes.label: Cross-border capital flows
nodes.description: The net movement of investment capital across jurisdictions into and out of financial assets, measured as a continuous flow rate.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite
nodes.description: The aggregate propensity of investors to accept risk in portfolios, measured continuously through allocation tilts and risk premia indicators.

nodes.label: Private credit spread
nodes.description: The yield premium demanded on privately originated credit instruments relative to a comparable risk-free benchmark, measured continuously.

nodes.label: Equity valuation pressure
nodes.description: The continuous tendencies for equity prices to compress or expand relative to fundamentals, proxied by price-to-earnings, earnings yields and market-implied returns.

nodes.label: Emerging market financial stress
nodes.description: The continuous degree of currency, bond and equity market strain in emerging economies, measured by exchange rate moves, yields and volatility.

nodes.label: Safe-haven asset flows
nodes.description: The rate at which capital is reallocated into traditionally defensive assets (e.g., precious metals, high-quality debt), measured as a continuous inflow/outflow metric.

nodes.label: Leverage in non-bank credit
nodes.description: The aggregate leverage ratio within non-bank credit intermediation (including private credit and shadow banking), measured as a continuous stock-like ratio.

nodes.label: Labor market tightness
nodes.description: The continuous balance between labor demand and supply, measured by vacancy-to-unemployment ratios and related wage-pressure indicators.

Armed conflict intensity
nodes.description: The overall magnitude and tempo of kinetic military operations and violence within the conflict zone.

nodes.label: Civilian displacement rate
nodes.description: The rate at which civilians are forced to leave or are uprooted from their habitual residences within affected areas.

nodes.label: Cross-border refugee flow
nodes.description: The volume and velocity of people crossing international borders seeking refuge as a result of the conflict.

nodes.label: Humanitarian aid delivery rate
nodes.description: The frequency and quantity of delivered humanitarian assistance (food, shelter, medical supplies) into affected populations.

nodes.label: Diplomatic tension level
nodes.description: The prevailing intensity of bilateral and multilateral diplomatic friction, public rebukes, and formal complaints between external actors.

nodes.label: Diplomatic sanctions and expulsions rate
nodes.description: The frequency of formal diplomatic measures such as expulsions, sanctions, or suspension of relations enacted in response to the conflict.

nodes.label: Multilateral engagement level
nodes.description: The intensity of involvement and activity of multilateral processes and forums (deliberations, resolutions, investigations) addressing the crisis.

nodes.label: Transnational security incident rate
nodes.description: The rate at which suspected plots, attacks, arrests, and cross-border security incidents linked to the conflict occur outside the primary combat zone.

nodes.label: Protest mobilization intensity
nodes.description: The level and frequency of public demonstrations, counter-demonstrations, and street-level mobilization related to the conflict in multiple jurisdictions.

nodes.label: Spillover violence rate
nodes.description: The frequency and scale of localized violent incidents (including communal violence, reprisals, and settler-related attacks) in neighboring or connected areas.

nodes.label: Allied security posture rigidity
nodes.description: The degree to which allied and partner states harden military readiness, base security measures, and posture in response to the conflict.

nodes.label: Information amplification velocity
nodes.description: The speed and breadth at which conflict-related information, narratives, and imagery propagate across media and social networks.

nodes.label: Foreign public polarization
nodes.description: The degree of polarization and intensity of opinion among external publics regarding actors, actions, and policies tied to the conflict.

nodes.label: Legal and accountability pressure intensity
nodes.description: The strength and frequency of legal initiatives, investigations, company listings, and accountability mechanisms triggered by conflict-related actions.

nodes.label: Border control stringency
nodes.description: The strictness and enforcement intensity of cross-border controls, entry restrictions, and migration policies in response to security and refugee flows.

nodes.label: Economic and energy market disruption level
nodes.description: The magnitude of disruptions in trade, energy markets, critical supply chains, and economic activity attributable to the conflict and its spillovers.

Rising diplomatic friction (sanctions, expulsions, formal protests) prompts the US and partners to tighten export controls, screen foreign AI vendors, and open inquiries/enforcement actions, raising the intensity and scope of regulatory scrutiny in the US–China tech competition.

Interruptions to transport and spare‑parts flows reduce availability of munitions, fuel and maintenance, degrading operational sustainment and forcing reductions in sortie rates and tempo of ground operations.

Logistical and settlement frictions from disrupted shipping and trade increase trading volatility and operational risk, leading dealers to reduce inventories and widen bid‑ask spreads, tightening fixed‑income market liquidity.

Logistical disruptions from the Russia–Ukraine conflict (insurance shocks, port congestion and longer voyages) reduce available tanker capacity and cause rerouting or delays, lowering crude volumes actually transiting narrow chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz in the near term.

War-related interruptions to semiconductor and specialized hardware shipments reduce some developers' access to accelerators needed for large-scale training, slowing or downsizing model training and lowering average deployed model capability in affected actors.

A rapid rise in deployed model capability enables more autonomous ISR and precision strike systems and faster decision loops, lowering operational thresholds and increasing the tempo and scale of kinetic operations between rivals.

Rapid improvements in deployed AI model capabilities raise market forecasts for near-term productivity, growth and inflation, leading participants to price in higher expected future central bank policy rates.

Improvements in deployed AI model capability for maritime ISR, anomaly detection and autonomous reconnaissance raise effective monitoring and attribution of hostile acts, strengthening deterrence and reducing the incidence of small-boat harassment and other disruptions.

Rising average model capability—driven by rivalry-driven R&D—enables more effective planning, target recognition, and guidance tools that actors can use to select and strike energy infrastructure, increasing outages and stress on energy supplies supporting Ukraine and its neighbours as those tools are fielded.

Accelerated deployment of autonomous surveillance and enforcement agents along contested borders and in occupied areas increases rates of misidentification and accidental engagements, producing localized clashes and reprisals that spill into neighboring communities.

Faster deployment of agentic trading and risk-monitoring systems intensifies algorithmic responses to Iran–US incidents, causing larger, quicker repricing and upward spikes in oil markets when standoff signals appear.

Heightened AI-focused regulation, export controls and enforcement increase compliance costs and legal uncertainty for foreign investors, causing them to reduce or reroute cross-border capital into jurisdictions perceived as higher regulatory risk.

Tighter regulatory scrutiny and export-control rulemaking tied to US–China rivalry create licensing delays and legal barriers that directly slow or block transfers of AI-enabled systems (drones, targeting software, logistics AI) from allies to Ukraine, reducing effective military support in the near term.

A surge of capital into AI equities, private rounds and infrastructure diverts demand away from long-duration sovereign and high-grade fixed income (portfolio rebalancing) and increases term premia, putting upward pressure on long-term nominal yields.

Increased capital flows into AI firms accelerate production and scaling of ISR, autonomous effectors, and logistics optimization systems that allies can procure or donate, thereby raising the quantity and capability of military assistance available to Ukraine within a production and procurement cycle.

High-frequency, high-profile cyber intrusions against AI infrastructure and sensitive networks that are attributed (or publicly blamed) on the opposing side trigger formal protests, sanctions, and expulsions, directly elevating bilateral and multilateral diplomatic friction.

Targeted cyberattacks that disable power, water, logistics or humanitarian coordination systems in conflict zones precipitate acute civilian suffering and infrastructure collapse, driving rapid cross-border population movements.

Rising cyber exploits that hit trading platforms, market-making systems or critical data feeds cause trading outages and prompt liquidity providers to pull back or widen quotes, directly degrading fixed-income market liquidity.

A rise in cyber exploits against AI-enabled navigation, port-automation and logistics platforms increases the frequency of successful attacks that halt or degrade vessel traffic and port operations in the Persian Gulf and nearby chokepoints, producing measurable transit disruptions.

Increased successful cyber operations against oil terminal control systems, SCADA and tanker-management platforms directly degrade throughput and force temporary shutdowns, lowering crude export volumes transiting key chokepoints.

An uptick in malicious cyber activity aimed at AI components (optimization/automation systems for ports, freight management, and defense logistics) causes outages and data corruption that produce measurable delays and rerouting in weapons and humanitarian supply chains into the conflict zone.

A sustained rise in long-term yields raises sovereign borrowing costs and forces fiscally constrained governments to delay/curtail defense procurement and contractor payments, reducing operational tempo and lowering near-term kinetic intensity.

Higher long‑term yields increase the opportunity and financing costs of holding inventories for both commercial and strategic actors, prompting drawdowns or reduced purchases that lower refined fuel stock levels.

Rising long‑term sovereign yields increase governments' debt‑service and borrowing costs, constraining discretionary budgets and leading to slower, smaller or delayed external military assistance and procurement for partners supporting Ukraine.

A sustained rise in long-term nominal yields raises financing and pension costs for firms and public bodies, prompting near-term cuts to IT/security operating budgets and reducing patching and monitoring, which increases the frequency and success of cyber exploits against AI systems.

Rising market-implied future policy rates increase discount rates and borrowing costs, compress VC valuations and fundraising, and cause institutional investors to pull back from high-growth tech allocations, directly reducing new capital flowing into AI startups and infrastructure.

Acute illiquidity in global fixed-income markets precipitates disorderly sovereign bond moves and targeted losses for foreign investors, prompting formal protests, investigations or sanctions claims between affected states and raising bilateral diplomatic friction.

Tightening in fixed‑income market liquidity raises short‑term funding and trade‑finance costs (commercial paper, repos and market‑making) used by shippers, freight forwarders and suppliers, forcing inventory cuts and payment delays that produce immediate logistical and supply‑chain interruptions.

Severe tightening in fixed-income market liquidity disrupts corporate and cloud-provider treasury operations and credit-backed procurement, delaying purchases/rental of large-scale compute and data-center capacity needed for training cutting-edge models, thereby slowing near-term increases in model capability.

A sudden negative swing in cross-border capital flows (capital flight or remittance stoppage) sharply reduces household income and fiscal capacity in a fragile conflict zone, triggering rapid deterioration of services and livelihoods that drives people to cross borders seeking refuge.

Higher cross-border capital inflows improve availability of trade finance, letters of credit and marine insurance for exporters and traders, enabling more tanker loadings and increasing crude volumes transiting key chokepoints.

A sudden pullback in cross‑border capital flows reduces trade finance and working capital available to energy traders and operators, causing delayed cargoes, curtailed imports and increased short‑term stress in energy supply chains for importing countries.

A rise in investor risk appetite lowers insurer and carrier risk premia for transits through contested waters, reducing commercial rerouting and the frequency/intensity of operational disruptions reported at maritime chokepoints.

A decline in investor risk appetite raises the cost and reduces availability of corporate financing and export‑credit/insurance for defense manufacturers and exporters, slowing deliveries and reducing the pace or volume of allied materiel shipments to Ukraine.

A decline in investor and corporate risk appetite leads firms to postpone or scale back production rollouts of experimental agentic AI systems to avoid potential operational, reputational and liability risks, lowering deployment rates.

A rapid escalation of kinetic operations raises uncertainty and tail-risk perceptions, prompting institutional and retail investors to de-risk portfolios and increase allocations to safe assets, thereby lowering aggregate risk appetite.

Heightened conflict drives order imbalances and volatility in regionally exposed sovereign and corporate bonds while dealer balance-sheet constraints and repo funding stress reduce market depth and widen bid-ask spreads.

Intensified kinetic operations (naval strikes, air attacks, missile barrages) in or near the Gulf/Red Sea directly threaten commercial shipping and prompt route suspensions or convoying that immediately increases maritime transit disruptions.

A sharp rise in frontline fighting and materiel losses creates immediate operational needs and political pressure that prompt allies to accelerate and expand weapons, ammunition, and logistics deliveries to sustain the defending force.

Increased kinetic operations and strikes against export nodes (ports, pipelines, Black Sea shipping) physically reduce flows and force rerouting, producing near-term supply shortfalls and price spikes for regional energy markets.

A spike in kinetic conflict raises incentives and operational cover for state and proxy actors to launch cyber operations against adversary AI infrastructure (model endpoints, data pipelines, control systems) to degrade battlefield automation, increasing cyber exploit frequency and severity.

Substantial and sustained refugee inflows raise host-country near-term fiscal spending and expected future debt issuance, increasing sovereign risk premia and pushing up long-dated government yields in affected markets.

Large, fast refugee movements create urgent border-management and humanitarian processing needs that governments and NGOs meet by procuring and fielding agentic systems (surveillance drones, autonomous triage/translation agents), accelerating deployment rates.

Rising diplomatic friction (sanctions, trade restrictions, reputational risk) causes fast, anticipatory portfolio reallocation and withdrawal of cross-border funding from exposed jurisdictions into safe-haven markets, producing net outflows.

Escalating diplomatic friction among states involved in the standoff prompts governments to enact sanctions, export controls, or emergency energy measures (e.g., SPR releases), increasing the intensity and frequency of official energy-market interventions.

Escalating diplomatic confrontations and public condemnations raise domestic political incentives for allied governments to demonstrate resolve by increasing or fast-tracking military assistance packages.

Rising diplomatic friction between states triggers near-term government actions—export controls, entity listings, mandatory vendor reviews and expanded investigations—directly increasing the intensity and scope of regulatory scrutiny on rival-country AI firms and services.

Elevated diplomatic tensions drive investors and policymakers to favor domestic or allied AI companies (reshoring, sanctions avoidance, preferential procurement), diverting capital away from adversary-linked firms and increasing flows into national/regime-aligned AI projects.

Rising localized attacks and sabotage around ports, terminals, and pipelines adjacent to strategic chokepoints force temporary closures or reduced throughput, directly cutting crude export volumes through those chokepoints.

Localized violent incidents on border routes, rail lines, or at transshipment hubs interrupt freight movements and create chokepoints that degrade commercial and military logistics serving the conflict zone.
